རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ཡོད་ན#། །འགོག་པ་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་#ནི་ཡོངས་གནས་ཕྱིར། །འགོག་ལ་#གནོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན། །ལམ་ལ་རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་ན་ནི། །སྒོམ་#པ་འཐད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཅི་#སྟེ་ལམ་དེ་བསྒོམ་བྱ་ན། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་མ་
ཡིན། །གང་ཚེ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཀུན་འབྱུང་དང་། །འགོག་པ་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན། །ལམ་གྱི་#སྡུག་བསྔལ་འགོག་པ་ནི། །གང་ཞིག་ཐོབ་པར་#འགྱུར་བར་འདོད། །གལ་ཏེ་རང་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ནི། །ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན། །དེ་#ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡོངས་ཤེས་འགྱུར། །
རང་བཞིན་གནས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནམ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ནི་ཁྱོད་ཉིད་ཀྱི#། །སྤང་དང་མངོན་དུ་བྱ་བ་དང་། །བསྒོམ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་དག་ཀྱང་། །ཡོངས་ཤེས་བཞིན་དུ་མི་རུང་ངོ་། །རང་བཞིན་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་ཡིས། །འབྲས་བུ་རང་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ནི། །ཐོབ་པ་མིན་
པ་གང་ཡིན་དེ#། །ཇི་ལྟར་འཐོབ་#པར་ནུས་པར་འགྱུར། །འབྲས་བུ་མེད་ན་འབྲས་གནས་མེད། །ཞུགས་པ་དག་ཀྱང་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །གལ་ཏེ་སྐྱེས་བུ་གང་ཟག་བརྒྱད། །དེ་དག་མེད་ན་དགེ་འདུན་མེད། །འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་རྣམས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། །དམ་པའི་
ཆོས་ཀྱང་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཆོས་དང་དགེ་འདུན་ཡོད་མིན་ན། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡོད་པར་འགྱུར། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་#སངས་རྒྱས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ། །མ་བརྟེན་པར་ཡང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་#བྱང་ཆུབ་སངས་རྒྱས་ལ། །མ་བརྟེན་པར་ཡང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར། །ཁྱོད་
ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ནི། །སངས་རྒྱས་མིན་པ་གང་ཡིན་དེས། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སྤྱོད་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཕྱིར། །བརྩལ་#ཀྱང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་མི་འགྱུར། །འགའ་ཡང་ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་མིན་པ། །ནམ་ཡང་བྱེད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ#། །མི་སྟོང་པ་ལ་ཅི་ཞིག་བྱ། །རང་བཞིན་ལ་ནི་བྱ་བ་
span: how could suffering exist? It was said that suffering is impermanent; it does not exist in an inherent nature. If it existed by nature, how could it ever arise? Therefore, for one who negates emptiness, the origin <note>the second noble truth</note> cannot exist. If suffering existed by nature, cessation <note>the third noble truth</note> would not exist. Because you hold it to be naturally established, you negate cessation. If the path had an inherent nature, meditation would not be tenable. If that path is to be meditated upon, it cannot have an inherent nature for you. When suffering, origin, and cessation do not exist, what cessation of suffering do you expect to attain through the path? If one does not have thorough knowledge <note>of suffering</note> by its very nature, how could it ever be thoroughly known? Does its nature not remain? Likewise, abandonment, realization, meditation, and the four fruits are also untenable for you, just like thorough knowledge. How could one be able to attain a fruit that is not attained by its own nature through the grasping of an inherent nature? If the fruits do not exist, those who abide in the fruits do not exist, and those who enter the paths do not exist. If the eight types of persons do not exist, then the Sangha does not exist. Because the noble truths do not exist, the Sublime Dharma also does not exist. If the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how could a Buddha exist? For you, it follows that a Buddha would exist without depending on awakening. For you, it also follows that awakening would exist without depending on a Buddha. For you, one who is not a Buddha by their own nature would not attain awakening even if they strove in the conduct of awakening for the sake of awakening. No one would ever perform Dharma or non-Dharma actions. What could an un-empty thing do? In an inherent nature, there is no activity.
head: If things were not dependently originated,
old_translation:
...how could suffering exist? That which was spoken of as "impermanent suffering" does not exist in an inherent nature.

If it existed through an inherent nature, how could it ever arise <note>since an inherent nature is fixed and unproduced</note>? Therefore, for one who harms <note>denies</note> emptiness, the origin of suffering does not exist.

If suffering existed by inherent nature, its cessation would not exist. Because you hold to inherent nature, you cause harm to cessation.

If the path had an inherent nature, meditation would not be tenable. If that path is to be meditated upon, it cannot have an inherent nature for you.

When suffering, its origin, and its cessation do not exist, then what "cessation of suffering" do you expect to attain through the path?

If thorough knowledge <note>of suffering</note> is not possible by its very nature, how could it ever become thorough knowledge? Does it not remain in its own nature?

In the same way, for you, abandoning, realizing, meditating, and the four fruits would be impossible, just as thorough knowledge was.

By holding to inherent nature, how could a fruit that was not previously attained by its own nature ever be attained?

If the fruits do not exist, those who abide in the fruits do not exist, nor do those who enter the paths. If those eight types of persons do not exist, then the Sangha does not exist. 

Because the noble truths do not exist, the holy Dharma also does not exist. If the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how could the Buddha exist?

It would follow for you that a Buddha exists without depending on enlightenment. It would also follow for you that enlightenment exists without depending on a Buddha.

For you, one who is not a Buddha by inherent nature could never attain enlightenment, even if they practiced for enlightenment.

No one would ever perform Dharma or non-Dharma. What could one do with the non-empty? An inherent nature cannot be acted upon.

<summary>Nagarjuna argues that if things had inherent nature, they would be static and unchangeable. This would make the spiritual path impossible, as suffering could not arise or cease, and a non-enlightened being could never become a Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>suffering, cessation, path, inherent nature, meditation, enlightenment, Buddha, Sangha, Dharma, four noble truths</keywords>
